paras.text: Bad Faith and Unfair Trade Practices, Audio Lecture

If you take one thing out of this chapter, take this. In Michigan the words bad faith get used loosely, and the law splits the idea into three separate tools. Mixing them up is the most common mistake in this entire area, and it is the mistake that makes a contractor or a homeowner sound like they do not know what they are talking about in front of an adjuster.
So we fix the framework first, and then everything else drops into one of three buckets.
Twelve ideas. After most of them, a question and then silence. Answer out loud.
Idea one. The three tools. Learn this before anything else.

Tool one is the penalty interest statute, M C L five hundred point two zero zero six. That is a private right. An insured can collect twelve percent interest on a late paid claim, with no bad faith lawsuit required. It is a mechanical calculation.

Tool two is the unfair trade practices list, M C L five hundred point two zero two six. Fourteen things an insurer is not supposed to do. The catch is that an insured cannot sue under it. It is enforced by the Department of Insurance and Financial Services, D I F S, administratively.

Tool three is common law bad faith, a tort suit. Michigan does not recognize that for a first party insured suing their own carrier. It survives only when a liability insurer refuses to settle within policy limits and an excess judgment lands on its own insured.
Say those back in one breath. Two zero zero six, private, twelve percent. Two zero two six, no private suit, D I F S enforces. Common law bad faith, third party only.
Every single thing in the rest of this chapter sorts into one of those three. When something confuses you later, come back and ask which bucket it is in.
Idea two. Section two zero zero six, subsections one and two.

Subsection one says the insurer must pay benefits on a timely basis to its insured, to a person directly entitled to benefits, or to a third party tort claimant, or in the alternative pay twelve percent interest on the late claim. Failing to do either one is an unfair trade practice, unless the claim is reasonably in dispute.

Now notice where that phrase reasonably in dispute sits, because its location is the whole ballgame later. It is in subsection one. And in subsection four it protects only a narrow category of claimant. Hold that thought, because in about five minutes it is going to decide a real argument for you.

Subsection two is a small housekeeping rule. If the insurer loses in court and pays the judgment plus the required interest, that alone is not an additional unfair trade practice. Paying what you were ordered to pay does not stack another violation on top.
Idea three. Subsection three, the clock everybody in claims work should have memorized.
The insurer must specify in writing exactly what documents constitute a satisfactory proof of loss within thirty days after receiving the claim, unless the claim settles inside those thirty days.
Then, once a satisfactory proof of loss is supplied, the insurer has sixty days from receiving it to pay the supported amount, or the payment is untimely.
Thirty and sixty. Two different clocks, doing two different jobs. Thirty days to tell you what it needs. Sixty days to pay once you have given it.

Let me walk the dates so it sticks. A fire claim is reported May first. The insurer has until roughly May thirty first to send the letter spelling out what it needs. Say the homeowner supplies everything on June fifteenth. The insurer then has until roughly August fourteenth to pay the supported amount.
Miss that, and subsection four is triggered.
Question. Claim reported March first, proof of loss materials letter due when, and if the homeowner delivers everything April tenth, when is payment late.
The letter is due by roughly March thirty first, thirty days after the claim. Payment is late after roughly June ninth, sixty days after the satisfactory proof of loss came in on April tenth.
Idea four. Subsection four, sentence one. This is the sentence that pays.

The first sentence of subsection four says that if benefits are not paid on a timely basis, the benefits paid bear simple interest, from a date sixty days after satisfactory proof of loss was received, at the rate of twelve percent per annum, if the claimant is the insured or a person directly entitled to benefits under the insured's insurance contract.
Now listen to what is missing from that sentence. No qualifier. No mention of whether the claim was disputed.
If you are the insured, or someone directly entitled to benefits under your own policy, and you get paid late, you get twelve percent. That is it.
This is the single most useful fact in the chapter for real claims work, and it is the one carriers most often talk past.
Idea five. Subsection four, sentence two, and why it is not yours.
The second sentence is where the reasonably in dispute language lives, and it applies only to third party tort claimants.

For one of them to get the same twelve percent, three things must all be true. The insurer's liability must not be reasonably in dispute. The insurer must have refused payment in bad faith. And a court of law must have determined that bad faith.
That is a much higher bar, and it belongs only to people who are not the policyholder but have a liability claim against someone the insurer covers.

So here is the trap, and it is the one adjusters run on homeowners constantly. An adjuster says, we do not owe you twelve percent because the claim is reasonably in dispute. If the person he is talking to is the insured, that defense is not in their sentence. It lives in the third party sentence. Different claimant, different rule.

Four other mechanics round out subsection four. Interest is paid on top of, and at the same time as, the loss payment. If the loss exceeds the policy limit, interest runs on the limit. If the insurer offers to pay, the claimant turns it down, and never recovers more than that offer, no interest is owed. And interest under this section is offset against any separate judgment interest the insurer owes.
Question. Your homeowner is the named insured, paid ninety days after a clean proof of loss, and the carrier says the claim was reasonably in dispute so no interest. What is your answer.

The reasonably in dispute limit is in the second sentence of subsection four, which covers third party tort claimants. She is the insured, so the first sentence governs, and she gets twelve percent simple interest running from sixty days after satisfactory proof of loss.
Idea six. Section two zero two six, the list, and the threshold that guards it.

The statute's own preamble sets the threshold, and it is worth memorizing close to verbatim. Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the business of insurance, other than isolated incidents, are a course of conduct indicating a persistent tendency to engage in that type of conduct.

Read that closely. D I F S is looking for a pattern, not a single bad claim file. One rough denial letter, standing alone, generally will not trigger an enforcement action, though it can still be evidence somewhere else.
The list runs fourteen items, lettered a through n. The ones that come up constantly in property claims are these.

Misrepresenting pertinent facts or policy provisions relating to coverage. Failing to acknowledge or act reasonably and promptly on claim communications. Failing to adopt reasonable standards for prompt investigation. Refusing to pay claims without a reasonable investigation based on the available information. Failing to affirm or deny coverage within a reasonable time after proof of loss is completed. Failing to attempt in good faith to settle promptly and fairly once liability has become reasonably clear. Compelling insureds to sue by offering substantially less than what is owed. Making a payment without stating what coverage it was paid under. Delaying investigation or payment by demanding duplicate paperwork purely to duplicate a verification already done. Failing to promptly settle one portion of a claim, where liability is clear, to pressure the insured on a different, disputed portion. And failing to give a reasonable, fact based, policy based explanation for a denial or a compromise offer.

That second to last one deserves a second of your attention, because you will see it. Holding up the part of the claim nobody disputes, in order to get leverage on the part somebody does dispute, is on the list by name.

Subsection two also requires insurers to keep a complete written record of every complaint since their last D I F S exam, with the number, the type, the outcome, and the time it took. Failing to keep that record is itself a violation.
Idea seven. How D I F S actually enforces a list nobody can sue under.
A pipeline runs through five sections, and knowing it tells you what a complaint really sets in motion.
Section two zero two eight lets the commissioner investigate on probable cause.

Section two zero two nine requires written notice of a hearing. But before that notice goes out, bureau staff must give the insurer a chance to confer informally, and the matter can be resolved summarily by agreement.

Section two zero three zero governs the hearing. The insurer may be represented by counsel and show cause why a cease and desist order should not issue. And here is the detail that surprises people: the burden of proof sits on the agency, not the insurer. The insurer may also request an independent hearing officer instead of the commissioner, and gets one dismissal of that officer within twenty days.

Section two zero three eight is where the money comes in. On a finding of violation after a hearing, the director issues written findings and a cease and desist order, and may impose a monetary penalty.

Here are the penalty pairs, and they are easy to swap by mistake. For an ordinary violation, one thousand dollars per violation, capped at ten thousand total. For a knowing violation, five thousand dollars per violation, capped at fifty thousand for all violations in any six month period. One and ten for ordinary. Five and fifty for knowing.
The director may also suspend or revoke the license for knowing, persistent violations, and order a refund of overcharges.

Section two zero four zero covers defying a cease and desist order that is already in effect. That runs up to twenty thousand dollars per violation, on top of suspension or revocation. And the order can never punish conduct predating it.
Question. Knowing violations, what is the per violation amount and the cap, and over what window.
Five thousand dollars per violation, capped at fifty thousand for all violations in any six month period. The one thousand and ten thousand pair is the ordinary violation.
Idea eight. Young, and what it did not say.

Young versus Michigan Mutual Insurance Company, nineteen eighty four. An insured tried three theories after a denied claim. A tort claim on section two zero zero six. A tort claim on section two zero two six. And a freestanding bad faith tort.

The court rejected all three. There is no implied private cause of action in tort for violation of section two zero zero six. And under section two zero two six, isolated incidents do not constitute unfair trade practices, because one insurance client's dealings with one company are, by their nature, an isolated incident. The insured does not have an independent cause of action under that section.
Now here is the nuance people miss, and it matters because it is the difference between having a remedy and not.

Young did not say an insured can never collect the section two zero zero six interest penalty. The same opinion notes that Michigan case law already lets a private party directly recover it. What is barred is dressing the claim up as an independent tort. The ordinary statutory interest claim is untouched.
So Young closes the tort door and leaves the interest door open. If somebody tells you Young means you cannot get the twelve percent, they have read it too fast.
Idea nine. Kewin, and getting the quote right.

Kewin versus Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Company, nineteen eighty, is the foundational no first party bad faith tort case. An insured sued for mental distress and exemplary damages after his disability insurer denied a claim.

Here is the court's actual language, because a common paraphrase gets it wrong. The court said, we decline to follow the California court and to declare the mere bad faith breach of an insurance indemnity contract an independent and separately actionable tort.

That is the real quote. You will often hear people describe Kewin's rule using the phrase wholly separate and independent duty, but that specific four word phrase is nowhere in the actual opinion. The underlying rule is the same either way, no independent tort without a duty that exists apart from the contract itself. But if you are asked to quote Kewin verbatim, use the actual words, an independent and separately actionable tort, not the borrowed phrase.

Watch the outcome too, because the numbers tell you how thoroughly the door closed. Kewin's insured kept only his contract money, sixteen thousand five hundred dollars on the disability policy plus seven hundred ninety eight dollars and forty cents on the life policy. The mental distress award stayed reversed and the fifty thousand dollar exemplary damages award was set aside.
Justice Williams wrote separately and would have allowed emotional distress contract damages. That opinion did not command the court, so do not quote it as the rule.
Idea ten. The one place bad faith really is a tort in Michigan.

Commercial Union Insurance Company versus Liberty Mutual Insurance Company, nineteen eighty six. This is about a liability insurer's duty to its own insured when there is a chance to settle within policy limits and an excess judgment could follow a refusal.
The court defined bad faith, for jury instruction purposes, as arbitrary, reckless, indifferent, or intentional disregard of the interests of the person owed a duty.

Two halves of that definition matter. Bad faith can exist without actual dishonesty or fraud, if the insurer is motivated by protecting its own interests at the insured's expense. And on the other side, honest mistakes, good faith denials, and simple negligence are not enough.

The court listed twelve non exclusive factors a jury may weigh, none decisive alone. Things like failing to keep the insured informed of settlement offers, failing to accept a reasonable within limits offer, ignoring the advice of an adjuster or attorney, and failing to investigate properly before refusing a settlement.
And it added a caution worth carrying into every file you ever review. Judge the insurer by what it knew at the time, not with twenty twenty hindsight.
Idea eleven. Griswold and Nickola, which lock the twelve percent down.
Back to the first party twelve percent rule, because two cases settle it.

Griswold Properties versus Lexington Insurance Company, two thousand seven, a special conflict panel, held that a first party insured is entitled to twelve percent penalty interest if a claim is not timely paid, irrespective of whether the claim is reasonably in dispute.

Then the Michigan Supreme Court in Nickola versus M I C General Insurance Company, five hundred Michigan one fifteen, two thousand seventeen, settled it in an underinsured motorist claim. An insured claiming under their own policy cannot be treated as a third party tort claimant under subsection four, so the reasonably in dispute exemption does not reach that claim. The court called this entirely consistent with Griswold and overruled an earlier Court of Appeals case that had gone the other way.
So if idea five felt like an argument, this is the authority behind it. Griswold at the Court of Appeals level, Nickola at the Supreme Court.
Idea twelve. Smith versus Globe, and a correction you will need.

Smith versus Globe Life Insurance Company, nineteen ninety nine, is often cited as proof that the Michigan Consumer Protection Act does not reach insurance at all. The actual opinion says almost the opposite on its own facts, which is exactly the kind of error that gets repeated because nobody opens the case.
Smith actually held two things.

First, and this half is still good law, the general exemption does cover the sale of insurance, because the test asks whether the general transaction is specifically authorized, not whether the specific misconduct is.

Second, under the statute as it then read, the court still let the insured's consumer protection claim over a credit life policy proceed, because the exemption then in place had its own built in exception for certain private actions. The claim survived summary disposition and was remanded.

The legislature closed that door shortly afterward, effective March twenty eighth, two thousand one. The current version, section four forty five point nine zero four, subsection three, says the Consumer Protection Act does not apply to, or create a cause of action for, conduct made unlawful by chapter twenty of the insurance code, for conduct occurring on or after March twenty eighth, two thousand one.
So today that route really is closed for chapter twenty claims. But get the reason right. Smith is the case that prompted the fix, not the case that states the current rule.
Idea thirteen. Two things that are not law, and one contrast.
Do not teach these as law, and do not let anyone sell them to you as law.

Senate Bill two forty five, from the twenty twenty five session, would add a new chapter thirty B titled the right to a civil cause of action against insurers for certain conduct. It would let a person damaged by a violation of section two zero zero six, two zero two six, or two zero two seven sue the insurer directly, with punitive and emotional distress damages if the violation was in bad faith, and a rebuttable presumption of bad faith from a two zero two six violation.

In other words, it would undo Kewin and Young by statute. That is a big deal, and it has not happened. As of the most recent check, it has only been reported favorably out of committee and referred to the Committee of the Whole in June of twenty twenty six. It has not passed either chamber. It is a bill, not a law.

And D I F S Bulletin two thousand twenty five, dash, twenty five, dash, I N S, issued October twenty fourth of twenty twenty five, reminds insurers about improper claims administration practices, quoting the same reasonable investigation and prompt settlement subsections we covered. It is written around automobile claims, not property, so treat it as guidance, not a property rule.
The contrast worth knowing: Florida has a real statutory first party bad faith law. Michigan has none. Only the twelve percent hammer and ordinary breach damages.
Time for the rapid fire recap. Fast, as a self check.

Thirty days to specify proof of loss materials. Sixty days after proof of loss to pay before interest starts. Twelve percent simple interest for the insured, no reasonably in dispute defense available to them. Fourteen enumerated unfair practices. Ten thousand dollars maximum aggregate penalty for ordinary violations, fifty thousand for knowing violations in a six month window, twenty thousand per violation for defying a cease and desist order. No first party bad faith tort. No private lawsuit under the unfair practices list. And Florida, for contrast, has a real statutory first party bad faith law. Michigan has none, only the twelve percent hammer and ordinary breach damages.
Know those cold and this chapter is yours. If any of the questions I asked gave you trouble, that is where to drill.
